messages.subject: Flying seabirds in DISTANCE sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
there is a larger discussion among seabird people on how to count and how
to deal with birds flying, e.g. snap shot counts, vector method.
For DISTANCE sampling on seabird line transects I have read that for flying
birds only the ones crossing the beam are to be counted.
What would be the reasoning for that ?
Are there any experiences from people that have tried several methods and
compared results, too ?

Thanks in advance and best regards
     Falk

messages.subject: Re: Flying seabirds in DISTANCE sampling
messages.body_plain:
> > there is a larger discussion among seabird people on how to count and how
> > to deal with birds flying, e.g. snap shot counts, vector method.
> > For DISTANCE sampling on seabird line transects I have read that for flying
> > birds only the ones crossing the beam are to be counted.
> > What would be the reasoning for that ?

That is a recommendation we put in the distance sampling book.  This
section is slightly revised in the new book, to appear in a few weeks.  It
works provided a) birds don't respond to the observation platform before
coming abeam and b) birds only cross the transect once during the time
that the survey is conducted.  Thus it won't work for birds milling
around, as they will tend to be detected closer to the trackline than they
would have been if you could have frozen the birds in a single location at
a snapshot moment.  I don't know if anyone is using this approach, but
would also be interested to hear of any comparative studies.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Z test
messages.body_plain:
I want to compare densities of Atlantic spotted dolphins between years and
between seasons.  I have calculated the Z statistic as described on p. 381
of the distance book, and have read the archived messages on the Z test.

The book suggests Z is approximately normally distributed, e.g. Z > 1.96
yields a p < .05.  Can you provide a reference for this use of the Z test?
When using a Z test or a t test to compare densities, how do we calculate
degrees of freedom?

Bob

messages.subject: Re: Z test
messages.body_plain:
> > I want to compare densities of Atlantic spotted dolphins between years and
> > between seasons.  I have calculated the Z statistic as described on p. 381
> > of the distance book, and have read the archived messages on the Z test.
> >
> > The book suggests Z is approximately normally distributed, e.g. Z > 1.96
> > yields a p < .05.  Can you provide a reference for this use of the Z test?
> > When using a Z test or a t test to compare densities, how do we calculate
> > degrees of freedom?

There are no df associated with the Z test - or rather, they are
infinite.  Hence, if sample size is small, the test is poor.  So what is
sample size?  In one sense, it is the number of individual detections -
schools in your case.  In another, it is the number of transect
lines.  Approximate df can be obtained using the Satterthwaite method (see
the book).  An approximate t-test can then be used.

This is better covered in our new book, due out in July (see our web
pages).  I will send separately the Latex code for the section dealing
with this.

messages.subject: Measuring distance in 3-dementions
messages.body_plain:
I'm developing a pilot study to estimate abundance and density of black
rockfish along a section of coastline in south-central Alaska.  I'll be
evaluating the use of mark-resighting closed population models and line
transect sampling to obtain independent estimates and to evaluate bias.
I'll be using SCUBA to do both.  Black rockfish are a pelagic species
commonly associated with bottom habitats but can occur off bottom.  They are
a schooling species so I may end up counting schools and estimating school
size instead of counting individual fish.  My main question is what is the
best technique to measure distance to an individual or school if the fish
are distributed 3-dementionally?  If I draw an imaginary line vertically to
the transect line and measure the perpendicular distance from myself to fish
both on the bottom and fish off the bottom than I'm dealing with a volume.
Alternatively, I could estimate the perpendicular distance from the
"imaginary vertical line" to the fish, whether they are off the bottom or
not.  This in my mind adds another delectability function, since not all
fish at a given perpendicular distance to the "imaginary vertical line" are
the same distance to the observer.   I could minimize this by swimming off
bottom a bit and ignoring fish that are and equal distance above me.  Do you
have suggestions?

Thanks, Mike
mike_...@fishgame.state.ak.us

messages.body_plain:
> > I'm developing a pilot study to estimate abundance and density of black
> > rockfish along a section of coastline in south-central Alaska.  I'll be
> > evaluating the use of mark-resighting closed population models and line
> > transect sampling to obtain independent estimates and to evaluate bias.
> > I'll be using SCUBA to do both.  Black rockfish are a pelagic species
> > commonly associated with bottom habitats but can occur off bottom.  They are
> > a schooling species so I may end up counting schools and estimating school
> > size instead of counting individual fish.  My main question is what is the
> > best technique to measure distance to an individual or school if the fish
> > are distributed 3-dementionally?  If I draw an imaginary line vertically to
> > the transect line and measure the perpendicular distance from myself to fish
> > both on the bottom and fish off the bottom than I'm dealing with a volume.
> > Alternatively, I could estimate the perpendicular distance from the
> > "imaginary vertical line" to the fish, whether they are off the bottom or
> > not.  This in my mind adds another delectability function, since not all
> > fish at a given perpendicular distance to the "imaginary vertical line" are
> > the same distance to the observer.   I could minimize this by swimming off
> > bottom a bit and ignoring fish that are and equal distance above me.  Do you
> > have suggestions?

Mike, you'll find theory for 3D line transects in the 1993 distance
sampling book.  Unfortunately, we can't assume that animals are uniformly
distributed with respect to distance from the line in the vertical
direction in your (or most) applications.  This complicates things, but
can in principle be addressed.  I'm not aware though that anyone has
developed, or is devloping, this methodology.  We have not pursued it
partly because we felt that it would not be relevant to the vast majority
of users of Distance (and partly through lack of funds!).  It might make a
nice PhD project for someone though.

What can you do meantime?  Provided you can ensure that the majority of
fish on or near the 'line' (which is now a 2D plane, from the bottom
vertically up to the surface) are detected, you can just record horizontal
distances from this plane, and analyse the data in the usual way.  Three
approaches occur to me, which may or may not be workable for your study:

a) do one survey for fish on the bottom, then a separate survey for fish
off the bottom.  Add the 2 abundance estimates together.

b) use 2 (or more) SCUBA divers, one covering bottom fish, and the
other(s) covering fish off the bottom, to ensure g(0) is close to 1.

c) survey bottom fish only;  separately conduct a survey to estimate the
proportion of time spent on the bottom by monitoring a sample of fish.  If
this proportion is p, and estimated density of fish on the bottom is D,
then the estimated density (numbers per unit area of sea) is D/p.  Of
course, this can be converted to numbers per unit volume if you feel that
makes more sense, but I would tend to stick with D.

Steve Buckland

This is because many other studies simply employ fixed-width transects (of many different widths) and assume that all birds are observed within the transect.

Obtaining an estimate of the proportion of birds detected can be obtained from the Distance output.  However, I would like to know, based on our detection function using all observations to 100 m, what proportion of birds were detected at 25, 50 and 75 m from the line.
> >
> > Would truncating the data to 25 m and and forcing the program to use the detection function and parameter estimates from the analysis using all the data provide a correct estimate of p at 25 m ?  I realize the SE and CIs would be wrong.
> >
> > Or is there a way to take the full model and estimate p for distances <=25 m, and possibly calculate a 95% CI using the var-cov matrix and delta method?  My detection functions are either hazard rate or half-normal with no adjustment terms.

Duane, you will find amongst the output in Distance the following:

 Model
    Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*A(1)**2))

              Point        Standard    Percent Coef.        95 Percent
  Parameter   Estimate       Error      of Variation     ConfidenceInterval
  ---------  -----------  -----------  -------------- --------------------
    A( 1)      8.391        1.420          16.93
    f(0)     0.14416      0.65386E-02       4.54      0.13187      0.15758
  ---------  -----------  -----------  -------------- --------------------

For the hazard-rate, it will look slightly different.  With no
adjustments, just substitute A(1)=8.391 (in this particular data set) into
k(y), and evaluate at the required distances.

To get ci's, you could select the bootstrap option in Distance, and
calculate the probabilities as above for each resample, using output from
the bootstraps.  This requires some programming external to Distance, and
you will need to check the Distance help files to see how to access output
from the resamples.

Steve Buckland
